one_liner: Rust's work-stealing async runtime; 1M sleeping tasks used 2.8x less peak memory than concurrencpp and 4x less than Asio.
what_it_does: Tokio is the standard asynchronous runtime for Rust: a multi-threaded work-stealing task scheduler, a reactor over epoll, kqueue or IOCP (through mio), a timer driver, async TCP/UDP sockets and sync primitives. You write async fns, start them with tokio::spawn (which returns a JoinHandle) and run them under #[tokio::main] or a runtime Builder. It is not a drop-in for Asio or concurrencpp: a C++ project would reach it only through FFI or by moving the concurrent service into Rust.
how_it_is_fast: Rust compiles each async fn into a stackless state machine whose size is fixed at compile time, and tokio::spawn moves that future into one heap block (the task Cell) together with its header, scheduler handle, task id and trailer. tokio::time::sleep keeps its timer entry inline in the future (an intrusive timer registered in a hierarchical timing wheel of 6 levels with 64 slots), so in tokio 1.28.2 a sleeping task is a single allocation with no separate stack or timer object. That is about 216 bytes per task in this run, against about 619 for concurrencpp and 872 for Asio (derived from page data as (RSS at 1M minus RSS at 1 task) / 1M, 1 KB = 1024 bytes).
when_to_use: Rust services that keep hundreds of thousands to millions of mostly idle tasks alive at once (connections waiting on I/O or timers), where per-task memory dominates.
Network servers and clients that want a multi-core work-stealing scheduler with no hand-written thread-to-io_context mapping.
Memory-constrained hosts running a large fan-out of timers or sleeps, since each sleep lives inside its task allocation.
Teams that can put the concurrent part of a system in Rust and talk to C++ over a socket or FFI boundary.
when_not_to_use: Small task counts: at 1 task tokio had the largest footprint (3,092 KB vs Asio 1,668 KB), and only at 10k tasks did it pull ahead (6,908 vs concurrencpp 7,840 and Asio 10,244 KB).
When throughput rather than memory is the goal: the catalogue's own echo-server sibling shows Boost.Asio C++20 coroutines slightly faster than Tokio.
CPU-bound or blocking work inside tasks: a task only yields at .await, so long computations stall a core thread; the crate docs route such code to spawn_blocking or a separate pool.
In-process use from a C++ codebase: it is a Rust crate with no C ABI, so integration means FFI glue or a separate process.
Wasm targets: only the sync, macros, io-util, rt and time features build there, 'full' fails to compile and timers can panic.

integration.dependencies: pin-project-lite; optional per feature: mio, bytes, parking_lot, socket2, libc, signal-hook-registry, windows-sys, tokio-macros
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85 on master (README: 1.54 onward); the 1.53.x LTS line needs Rust 1.71; the benchmark used tokio 1.28.2
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows, Android (API 21), macOS, iOS and FreeBSD guaranteed; other mio platforms best effort; Wasm limited
integration.thread_safety: tokio::spawn on the default multi-thread runtime requires Send + 'static futures and moves tasks between worker threads; spawn_local and the current-thread runtime cover !Send futures.

gotchas: The measured version predates task padding: PR #5809 (merged 2023-06-21, after the 1.28.2 release the benchmark locked) makes the task Cell repr(align(128)) on x86-64, aarch64 and powerpc64 to avoid false sharing, so on current tokio each task allocation is rounded up to a multiple of 128 bytes. Per-task memory today is probably above the about 216 bytes seen here. Not re-measured, and the change is not in the changelog.

Peak RSS mixes fixed runtime cost with per-task cost. Tokio's multi-thread runtime starts one core thread per CPU (8 on this i7-8550U), while the Asio program runs everything on the main thread and concurrencpp uses one worker_thread_executor plus its timer_queue. The slope between the 1-task and 1M-task rows is the fairer comparison, and it still favours tokio about 2.9x over concurrencpp and 4x over Asio (derived).

The C++ programs are one design each and were not tuned: every Asio task builds its own asio::steady_timer inside an awaitable frame launched by co_spawn, and every concurrencpp task copies two shared_ptrs into its frame and makes its own delay object. Shared timers or custom frame allocators were not tried, the C++ library versions were unpinned (fetched at HEAD in June 2023) and the compiler is not named.

Single unreported-count runs of /usr/bin/time under WSL Ubuntu 20.04 on a laptop, memory only (no spawn time or wake latency), from a 4-star one-person repo; the tokio project itself makes no C++ comparison.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this entry when the deciding factor is the memory cost of very many concurrent tasks: the Tokio echo-server sibling covers throughput, where Asio is slightly ahead. GHC lightweight threads and Go goroutines are measured against OS threads or a pthread-based ring rather than C++ coroutine libraries, so this is the only sibling that compares stackless tasks with C++20 coroutine runtimes.
verified_claims_summary: Peak RSS from /usr/bin/time for N tasks each awaiting a 10 s timer, all alive at once, on an Intel i7-8550U (8 GB, WSL Ubuntu 20.04): tokio 1.28.2 (cargo --release) used 214,136 KB at 1M tasks versus 605,972 KB for concurrencpp and 853,144 KB for Asio (C++20 Release builds, compiler not named, libraries at June 2023 HEAD), about 2.8x and 4.0x less. Libunifex hung at 100k and above, and tokio was the largest at 1 task.
status_note: Tokio is very active (MIT, 33.4k stars, monthly minor releases, LTS lines 1.51.x to March 2027 and 1.53.x to September 2027); the evidence is a one-off June 2023 hobby benchmark against tokio 1.28.2, and current tokio's 128-byte task alignment may narrow the measured gap.
